newsitem.title: SUDAN: War seems far away from Sudanese capital.
newsitem.headline: War seems far away from Sudanese capital.

text.p: In the streets of the Sudanese capital the war in the east seems far away. Some Sudanese say they believe the government line that Ethiopians have invaded, others are sceptical or just don't want to know.

In Omdurman's bustling market on the west bank of the White Nile, the air is fragrant with mint and citrus and the traders are more interested in a hard sell than in tough talk about jihad (holy war) and international conspiracies.
"Never mind, try this," said Atoma, brushing aside a question about politics as she pours a capful of homemade perfume from a dusty old Johnnie Walker whisky bottle for a potential customer.
Here the only sign that Africa's largest country is at war was a pair of soldiers sharing a motorcycle, their faces strangely covered with surgical masks against the dust.
They were outnumbered by throngs of reed-thin men and women, draped in spotless white gowns, striding evenly along the dirt roads with sacks of produce balanced on their heads.
Merchants lazily swatted flies from stacks of tomatoes, aubergines and carrots or dozed in the heat on rickety wooden benches outside their shops.

The war was very distant, some said. But others echoed the rhetoric of the Khartoum government, saying the attacks on the army were an anti-Islamic plot inspired by the West, Israel and Sudan's neighbours.
"We didn't have any problem with any neighbours of the Sudanese," said date merchant Mohammad Saleh. "We only raised the flag of Islam. This is the problem, because we are Moslems."
"We can go into jihad now," he added, referring to President Omar Hassan al-Bashir's call for general mobilisation after an alliance of northern and southern rebels attacked in the east.
The government insists that Ethiopian and Eritrean forces are doing the fighting but all other parties dismiss this as an attempt to win Arab and international sympathy.

Bashir, a tailor, said: "We have no problem with the south. There is no difference between Christians and Moslems here. We are all Sudanese but foreign countries want to see Sudan split. Israel wants to be against us. The problem is not inside Sudan."

Southern rebels have been fighting the Moslem and Arabised government in the north since 1983. Moslem northerners, after seven years waiting for the Islamist military government to fall, have now joined the rebels on the battlefield.
Salah Abdel-Aziz, 42, who used to drive a taxi in Florida and now sells textiles in Omdurman market, took a more detached view of events on the Ethiopian border.
"Something happened over there. We hear it's Ethiopia or Eritrea. But I'm not sure of what happened exactly," he said.
"From what I hear on the television, you can believe what they say. But when I look at a foreign channel, I say Eritrea and Ethiopia have nothing to do with it," he added.

"If this happened with Eritrea and Ethiopia, everybody here in Sudan should go to the east. But if it is for something else...that's something different," said Abdel-Aziz, who has three boys under the age of conscription.
The Sudanese government media on Tuesday were full of news of the country preparing for war.
Newspaper headlines trumpeted messages of support from countries including Iran, like Sudan on the U.S. list of states which support what Washington calls "international terrorism".
The government says batches of volunteers are on their way to the fronts at Damazin to the south and Kassala to the east.
But down the road from the White Nile bridge, close to where the White Nile from Uganda merges the Blue Nile from Ethiopia, young men chatted in groups or lay on blankets reading books.
Mohammad Hamid, a university student, said he preferred to talk about religion or life in America than about Sudan's war.
"The war has not appeared here," he said of Khartoum. People are worried but want peace, he added.
